result:
Before I write it up, there's one bigger choice about how the guide gets built: where it lives and how volunteers get recordings into it. That choice shapes most of the design.

**1. Build it into the existing museum website (recommended).** Each exhibit gets a page on the current Eleventy site, and its code points there. Volunteers sign in to a simple web editor attached to the site, pick the exhibit and language, and upload the recording. The cleanup (levelling the volume, trimming the silences) runs automatically each time the site rebuilds on Netlify. There's no new service to pay for or look after, and the codes use the museum's own web address. The trade-off is that a new recording takes a few minutes to go live, and the site's files grow by a couple of hundred megabytes of audio.

**2. A separate small upload app.** This would sit alongside the site, with its own storage, and clean up each recording the moment it's uploaded. Recordings go live instantly, and the website stays untouched. The trade-off is a second system, with its own logins and running costs, for someone to maintain after I've gone.

**3. A ready-made museum audio guide service.** I'd drop this one. It means a subscription and someone else's look, and Welsh support is patchy.

I recommend 1. At ten new stories a year, waiting a few minutes for one to go live costs almost nothing. Fewer moving parts also matters, since it's volunteers who'll be using this.

On size: this is a project, so I'll write a full design document in the repository. A reviewer will read it before you do, and I may come back once with a few questions.

Which way do you want to go?
